title: The parallel postulate need not be kept

body: Euclid's Elements, in the text linked from Wikisource, builds plane geometry on postulates. One of them, the parallel postulate, is less obvious than the others, and for centuries geometers tried to derive it from the rest. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on nineteenth-century geometry records the break. In the 1820s Nikolai Lobachevsky and János Bolyai, working independently, built geometries on the negation of that postulate. Lobachevsky called his system imaginary geometry. Once those systems were shown to be as consistent as Euclid's, "the" geometry of mathematics was no longer a single structure. Whether physical space matches Euclid became, for some of the people the entry discusses, an experimental question, and others replied that experiments already presuppose a geometry. The mathematical existence of the alternatives is not in dispute. Which geometry fits a given physical theory is a further question. General relativity answers one version of it with a geometry that is not Euclid's.
said_by: Lobachevsky and Bolyai in the 1820s, as surveyed by the Stanford Encyclopedia
